title: From Strategies to Principles: My Journey Through Deimplementation
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: A teacher reflects that the biggest improvement in his practice came from subtraction rather than from any single strategy such as retrieval practice or explicit instruction. He argues for deimplementation: when a cognitive-science-aligned practice arrives, ask what it replaces rather than how to fit it in. He admits he long confused engagement with learning and spent enormous effort on elaborate activities that produced little. He also names the emotional cost, regret over past lessons, and reframes it as responsibility. The essay's central move is to shift from asking which strategy to use to asking which principle should guide a decision, so that practices change when beliefs do. It is a personal, practitioner-level case for principle-led instruction and lighter workload.
points: The biggest gain came from learning what to remove: asking what a new practice can replace reduced workload while improving learning.
Engagement, fun and busyness were weak proxies for learning, and chasing them produced complicated planning and little retention.
Regret over earlier teaching is reframed as responsibility: you cannot apply knowledge you do not yet have.
Two filter questions, what problem will this solve and what new problems might it create, govern every adoption decision.
Replacing the beliefs behind a strategy matters more than swapping one strategy for another, so principles should precede practices.
quotes: Like many teachers, I spent years believing that becoming a better teacher meant continually accumulating new ideas. Every meeting introduced another strategy. Every book offered another model.

The idea of “replace, don’t add” completely changed my thinking. Every time I encountered a practice that was more consistent with what cognitive science tells us about learning, I stopped asking, “How can I fit this into everything I’m already doing?

In reality, I had confused engagement with learning. Many of the instructional decisions I made were based on poor proxies for learning rather than on an understanding of how working memory, attention, and remembering actually work.
I cannot apply knowledge I do not yet possess. None of us know what we do not know until we know it. This perspective helped move my feeling from guilt to responsibility.

Those experiences led me to two questions that now form the foundation of every teaching decision I make: What problem will this solve? and What new problems might this create? Those questions have become my supreme filter for all my implementation and deimplementation processes.
Changing my teaching therefore required more than simply replacing one strategy with another. It required replacing the beliefs that justified using those strategies in the first place.
Instead, I ask, “What principle should guide this decision?” Programs, frameworks, and packaged solutions come and go as they always do, but my principles can and should endure.
